div.div:
NMIs always ends in device reset to avoid IRQ hazards or race conditions, as they are able to interrupt other ISRs mid-execution.
Additionally, NMIs are often indicators of critical errors, in which a Safe State transition is advisable.

div.div: The framework does not use level 1 interrupts by default, but the user can configure one interrupt source as level 1. In that case, it is the responsibility of the user to handle any potential race conditions / hazards. The recommended use case for a level 1 interrupt is safety critical operation of the application outside the scope of the safety framework interrupt task managers that is not connected to the error controller or NMI.

div.div: Redundant Handling: Most safety module error interrupts sources are connected to the error controller, which can be configured to issue redundant interrupts. There is no guarantee which interrupt will trigger first. Therefore, the tasks called in each ISR must handle this race condition by clearing both the interrupt flag source and the error control channel, to prevent execution of the other redundant ISR.

div.div: Level 0 interrupts can be interrupted by a level 1 interrupt.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 368px; height: 1px; padding-top: 755px; margin-left: 662px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0px; text-align: left;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: rgb(0, 0, 0); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; overflow-wrap: normal;

div.div: If an interrupt source is accidentally enabled without an ISR, the compiler will run a default handler. This default handler jumps to the beginning of the program, effectively causing an unsafe device reset (i.e., without going into a Safe State). To mitigate this, the default handler is replaced with a task that reports the error to the Error Handler. The Error ID is assumed to be configured to CRITICAL and will thus result in a safe device reset.
